name: Interest-only payment
whatItIs: This is the interest a borrower owes for one billing month on an interest-only loan. It answers: what is this month's bill? The lender charges a daily rate on the funded balance for each actual day.
analogy: It works like a parking meter: a fixed charge per day, so a 31-day month costs more than a 30-day month.

variables.name: Funded balance
variables.definition: The principal outstanding during the month, after any draws.
variables.sourceDocument: Loan servicing report

variables.name: Annual note rate
variables.definition: The yearly interest rate written in the note.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Days in the period
variables.definition: Actual calendar days in the billing month. The funding day counts; the payoff day does not.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: This is a cost to the borrower, not a test, so there is no safer direction. Check it against the servicing bill each month. The billing basis is set in the Model Credit Policy, Pricing structure.
commonSlips: Why not divide the yearly interest by 12? Months have 28 to 31 days. Dividing by 12 undercharges every 31-day month.
Which balance do I use? Use the funded balance, not the full commitment, unless the note charges the full commitment from day one.
Can I round the daily rate first? No. Keep the daily rate unrounded and round the month's total to the cent once.
takeaways: Interest = funded balance × rate ÷ 360 × actual days.
A 31-day month costs more than a 30-day month at the same rate.
Round once, at the end, to the cent.

name: Amortizing payment
whatItIs: This is the level monthly payment that repays a loan over its amortization period. It answers: what does the borrower pay each month on a term loan? Each payment covers that month's interest and repays some principal.
analogy: It is like paying off a phone over 25 years in equal instalments, where the early ones are mostly interest.

variables.name: Loan amount
variables.definition: The principal at the start of the amortization.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Annual note rate
variables.definition: The yearly rate in the note. The monthly rate is this rate ÷ 12.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Amortization
variables.definition: The number of monthly payments used to set the payment. It is often longer than the loan term.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: Here ROUND is part of the rule, not display: the note fixes the payment at the cent. Debt service and balance cells must use this rounded payment.

readTheResult: A higher payment means less cash left for the owner, so coverage is lower. The payment feeds annual debt service and coverage tests. The payment basis is set in the Model Credit Policy, Pricing structure.
commonSlips: Why does my payment look far too high? You may have used the loan term (say 10 years) instead of the amortization (say 25 years).
Do I enter the annual rate? No. Divide the annual rate by 12 for a monthly payment.
Should the payment change in a 31-day month? No. The payment is set on 12 equal months. Day count affects interest accrual only.
takeaways: The payment is set on 12 equal months: monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12.
Use the amortization, not the term, for the number of payments.
Round the payment to the cent, then use that rounded figure everywhere.

name: Annual debt service
whatItIs: Annual debt service is the total of a year's scheduled loan payments. It answers: how much debt cost must the property's income cover each year? It is the bottom of every coverage ratio.
analogy: It is the year's rent the property pays to the bank.

variables.name: Monthly payment
variables.definition: The scheduled payment, rounded to the cent, from the amortizing payment formula.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Loan balance (interest-only loans)
variables.definition: The balance used for an interest-only loan's yearly cost.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Annual note rate (interest-only loans)
variables.definition: The yearly rate in the note. Tests use the plain yearly rate.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: ROUND here applies the rule that the payment is fixed at the cent before × 12. For an interest-only loan use =B1*B2 and leave it unrounded.

readTheResult: Lower debt service is safer, because more income is left after paying the loan. It is the denominator of the coverage ratio. The tests that use it are in the Model Credit Policy, Rules for all commercial loans and Rules for all multifamily loans.
commonSlips: Why does my debt service differ by a few cents from the schedule? Round the monthly payment to the cent first, then multiply by 12.
Why not use the interest actually billed? Tests use the plain yearly rate (loan × rate) so every loan is compared the same way. Billed interest on actual days is slightly higher.
takeaways: Amortizing loan: debt service = rounded monthly payment × 12.
Interest-only loan: debt service = balance × annual rate.
Use the same debt service figure in every test for the same loan.

name: Loan constant
whatItIs: The loan constant is annual debt service per dollar of loan. It answers: how much yearly payment does each dollar borrowed cost? It lets you size a loan before you know the amount.
analogy: It is the price tag per dollar borrowed: 8.5 cents a year for every dollar.

variables.name: Annual debt service
variables.definition: Twelve rounded monthly payments for the loan.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Loan amount
variables.definition: The loan the debt service was worked out on.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: Show at least six decimals. Never round the constant before using it to size a loan; sizing divides by the unrounded cell. Without a loan amount, =12*PMT(rate/12,months,-1) gives the same constant to six decimals.

readTheResult: A lower constant is safer for the lender, because the same income supports more loan. Compare it with the cap rate: a constant above the cap rate means debt costs more than the property yields. No policy limit applies to the constant itself.
commonSlips: Is the constant just the note rate? Only for an interest-only loan. Amortization adds principal repayment, so the constant is higher.
Can I round it to two decimals? No. A constant of 8.48% instead of 8.4814% moves a loan size by thousands of dollars.
takeaways: Loan constant = annual debt service ÷ loan amount.
On an amortizing loan it is higher than the note rate.
Keep at least six decimals and size with the unrounded value.

name: Per diem interest
whatItIs: Per diem interest is one day's interest on the loan. It answers: what does each extra day cost? Closers and servicers use it for odd days at closing, payoffs and late payments.
analogy: It is the nightly rate on a hotel room you keep adding nights to.

variables.name: Balance
variables.definition: The principal outstanding on that day.
variables.sourceDocument: Loan servicing report

variables.name: Annual note rate
variables.definition: The yearly rate in the note.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: Show the per diem to the cent, but multiply days by the unrounded cell. Rounding first and then multiplying by many days lets the error grow.

readTheResult: It is a cost per day, so there is no pass or fail. It tells the borrower what a delay costs and the closer what to collect. The interest basis is set in the Model Credit Policy, Pricing structure.
commonSlips: Why 360 and not 365? The note bills Actual/360: a 360-day year with actual days counted. Using 365 undercharges.
Can I round the per diem and multiply it by 45 days? No. Multiply the unrounded daily figure, then round the total once.
takeaways: Per diem = balance × rate ÷ 360.
It changes whenever the balance changes, for example after a draw.
Use the unrounded per diem in any multi-day total.

name: Origination points
whatItIs: Points are an upfront fee charged as a percent of the loan. It answers: how much does the lender collect at closing for making the loan? One point is 1% of the total commitment.
analogy: It is a cover charge at the door, sized by how big the party is.

variables.name: Points

commonSlips: Do points apply to the first advance or the whole loan? Check the term sheet. Ours charges the total commitment.
Is one point 0.1%? No. One point is 1% of the commitment.
takeaways: Fee = commitment × points ÷ 100.
One point = 1% of the commitment.
Points add to cash to close and raise the lender's yield.

name: Gross potential rent
whatItIs: Gross potential rent is the rent a property would earn in a year if every unit were leased at its scheduled rent. It answers: what is the ceiling on rental income? Everything below it is a deduction.
analogy: It is a full house at a theatre: the takings if every seat sells at the ticket price.

variables.name: Scheduled monthly rent per unit
variables.definition: The in-place rent for leased units and market rent for vacant units, each labelled.
variables.sourceDocument: Rent roll

inExcel.note: With one row per unit on the rent roll, use =SUM(rent column)*12 instead. Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: Gross potential rent is a ceiling, not a forecast. A higher figure is not safer by itself. Check it against the rent roll and market rents before you deduct vacancy.
commonSlips: Can I mix in-place and market rents? Yes, but label each. Unlabelled mixing hides a jump to market rent.
Do concessions or parking fees go here? No. Concessions reduce rent. Fees and parking are other income, added later.
takeaways: Gross potential rent = scheduled monthly rents × 12.
It is the most the property could earn from rent.
Other income and concessions stay out of it.

name: Vacancy and credit loss
whatItIs: Vacancy and credit loss is the income lost to empty space and unpaid rent. It answers: how much of the gross rent will not be collected? Underwriting uses the highest of actual, market or the policy minimum.
analogy: It is the empty seats and the bounced cheques at the theatre.

variables.name: Gross potential income
variables.definition: Scheduled rent for the year, plus recoveries where leases pass costs to tenants.
variables.sourceDocument: Rent roll

variables.name: Vacancy and credit loss rate
variables.definition: The greatest of actual vacancy, market vacancy and the policy minimum.
variables.sourceDocument: Appraisal excerpt (market vacancy), checked against the rent roll and the policy minimum

inExcel.note: MAX picks the greater rate, so the minimum is never added on top. Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: A higher vacancy allowance is more conservative. The minimum rate is set in the Model Credit Policy, Rules for all commercial loans and Rules for all multifamily loans. Never go below it.
commonSlips: Should I add the minimum to actual vacancy? No. Take the greater of the two, not the sum.
Is physical occupancy enough? No. Unpaid rent counts as loss too, so economic vacancy can be higher than empty units suggest.
takeaways: Vacancy = gross potential income × vacancy rate.
Use the greatest of actual, market and the policy minimum.
Unpaid rent is a loss even when the unit is full.

name: Effective gross income
whatItIs: Effective gross income is the income the property should actually collect in a year. It answers: after vacancy, what comes in? It is gross potential income, less vacancy, plus other income.
analogy: It is the theatre's real takings: full-house sales, less empty seats, plus the snack bar.

variables.name: Gross potential income
variables.definition: Scheduled rent (and recoveries) if fully leased.
variables.sourceDocument: Rent roll

variables.name: Vacancy and credit loss
variables.definition: Income lost to empty space and unpaid rent.
variables.sourceDocument: Appraisal excerpt, checked against the rent roll

variables.name: Other income
variables.definition: Recurring income such as fees, parking or laundry.
variables.sourceDocument: T-12 operating statement

inExcel.note: Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: Higher income is better, but only if it is real and recurring. It is the top line for net operating income. Income rules are in the Model Credit Policy, Rules for all commercial loans and Rules for all multifamily loans.
commonSlips: Should I apply vacancy to other income too? Only once. Do not take vacancy off other income twice.
Can a one-time lease buyout count? No. Count only income that recurs each year.
takeaways: Effective gross income = gross potential income − vacancy + other income.
It is the top line of the operating statement.
Count only recurring income.

name: Net operating income
whatItIs: Net operating income is the property's cash flow before loan payments. It answers: what does the property earn from operations in a year? It drives value, debt yield and coverage.
analogy: It is the shop's profit before the owner pays the mortgage.

variables.name: Effective gross income
variables.definition: Income after vacancy, plus other income.
variables.sourceDocument: T-12 operating statement

variables.name: Operating expenses
variables.definition: Taxes, insurance, management, repairs, utilities and payroll. The greater of the trailing 12 months and the appraiser's estimate.
variables.sourceDocument: T-12 operating statement, compared with the appraisal excerpt

inExcel.note: MAX applies the greater-of rule for expenses. Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: Higher net operating income is safer, if the income and expenses are realistic. The Model Credit Policy, Rules for all commercial loans and Rules for all multifamily loans set the greater-of expense rule and a management fee floor.
commonSlips: Do loan payments or depreciation come off? No. Net operating income is before debt service, depreciation and income tax.
The owner manages the property. Can I leave out management? No. Include a market management fee; a buyer or receiver would pay one.
takeaways: Net operating income = effective gross income − operating expenses.
Use the greater of actual and appraised expenses.
Leave out debt service, depreciation and income tax.

whatItIs: The debt service coverage ratio shows how many times the property's income covers its loan payments. It answers: can the property pay its debt from its own income, with room to spare?
analogy: It is how many times your pay covers your rent: 1.3 times means you have 30% to spare.

1.2495x shows as 1.25x. Does it pass a 1.25x minimum? No. Compare at full precision; it fails.

Below 1.00x, income cannot pay the debt.

name: Break-even occupancy
whatItIs: Break-even occupancy is the share of gross rent needed to pay expenses and debt service. It answers: how empty can the property get before it cannot pay its bills?
analogy: It is the number of seats the theatre must sell to cover the lights and the loan.

variables.name: Operating expenses
variables.definition: Underwritten yearly expenses.
variables.sourceDocument: T-12 operating statement

variables.name: Annual debt service
variables.definition: Twelve rounded monthly payments.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Gross potential income
variables.definition: Scheduled income if fully leased.
variables.sourceDocument: Rent roll

inExcel.note: Keep the ratio unrounded and format the cell as a percentage. Compare it with a limit at full precision. Use ROUND only in a separate display cell.

readTheResult: Lower is safer. The cushion is actual occupancy minus break-even. There is no policy limit; it gives context for the vacancy rules in the Model Credit Policy, Rules for all commercial loans.
commonSlips: Can I leave out debt service? No. That gives operating break-even only, which hides the loan's risk.
Which occupancy do I compare? Economic occupancy, which counts unpaid rent as empty.
takeaways: Break-even = (expenses + debt service) ÷ gross potential income.
The cushion is occupancy minus break-even.
Above 100% means the property cannot break even even when full.

name: Capitalization rate
whatItIs: The cap rate links a property's income to its value. It answers: what yield does the price give, or what is the income worth? Value = net operating income ÷ cap rate.
analogy: It is the interest rate on a savings account, read backwards to find the balance.

variables.name: Net operating income
variables.definition: Yearly income before debt service.
variables.sourceDocument: Appraisal excerpt

variables.name: Value
variables.definition: The appraised value for the same income state (as-is or stabilized).
variables.sourceDocument: Appraisal excerpt

readTheResult: A lower cap rate means a higher value for the same income, and less room if rates rise. The appraiser sets the rate; see the Model Credit Policy, Third-party reports. Match the income state to the value state.
commonSlips: Can I cap next year's income and call it today's value? No. That is a stabilized value, not an as-is value.
What if the cap rate is below the loan constant? Then debt costs more than the property yields. That is negative leverage.
takeaways: Cap rate = net operating income ÷ value.
Lower cap rate, higher value.
Use as-is income with as-is value and stabilized with stabilized.

analogy: It is how much of the house the bank owns on day one.

On a purchase, value = lower of price and appraisal.

name: Net funding wire
whatItIs: The net funding wire is the money the lender sends to the closing agent. It answers: how much leaves our account at closing? It is the initial funding less what the lender keeps.
analogy: It is your paycheck after deductions: the gross is the loan, the net is the wire.

variables.name: Initial funding
variables.definition: The advance made at closing.
variables.sourceDocument: Term sheet

variables.name: Points
variables.definition: Origination fee, on the commitment.
variables.sourceDocument: Settlement statement

variables.name: Other lender fees
variables.definition: Lender fees collected at closing.
variables.sourceDocument: Settlement statement

variables.name: Prepaid interest
variables.definition: Interest from funding to month-end.
variables.sourceDocument: Settlement statement

variables.name: Escrows and reserves held
variables.definition: Tax and insurance cushion, repair escrow and other reserves the lender holds.
variables.sourceDocument: Settlement statement

inExcel.note: Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: It is an amount, not a test. The settlement statement's sources must equal its uses. A negative wire means the deal is built wrong. Closing rules are in the Model Credit Policy, Third-party reports, under closing.
commonSlips: Do I wire the full advance? No. Net out what the lender keeps.
Should I net a cost the borrower pays a third party? No. Only items the lender keeps come off the wire.
takeaways: Wire = initial funding − points − fees − prepaid interest − escrows held.
Sources must equal uses.
A negative wire means stop and recheck.

name: Foreclosed property carrying value and charge-off
whatItIs: When the lender takes title, it books the property at fair value less cost to sell, capped at the loan. It answers: what is the property worth on our books, and what loss do we take now?
analogy: It is marking a trade-in at what the dealer will really pay, after its costs.

variables.name: Recorded loan amount
variables.definition: The loan balance on the books at title.
variables.sourceDocument: Loan servicing report

variables.name: Fair value
variables.definition: Value from a new appraisal at title.
variables.sourceDocument: Updated valuation for resolution

variables.name: Cost to sell
variables.definition: Estimated broker, legal and closing costs to sell.
variables.sourceDocument: Updated valuation for resolution

inExcel.note: Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: A smaller charge-off is better. Later falls in value are written down; rises are not booked until sale. The rule is in the Model Credit Policy, Extensions and default.
commonSlips: Gross value or value less cost to sell? Value less cost to sell.
Can I use the original appraisal? No. Order a new one at title.
takeaways: Carrying value = lower of the loan and fair value less cost to sell.
Charge-off = loan − (fair value − cost to sell), if positive.
Re-test value often; write down falls, never book rises.

name: Bucket headroom
whatItIs: Headroom is the largest new loan a concentration bucket can take before it breaches its cap. It answers: how much room is left in this bucket? A new loan adds to both the bucket and the base.
analogy: It is how much more water a glass can take when the glass grows a little as you pour.

variables.name: Cap
variables.definition: The bucket's maximum share of its base.
variables.sourceDocument: Model Credit Policy, Concentration, exceptions and approval authority

variables.name: Base commitments
variables.definition: Total commitments for the base the cap uses.
variables.sourceDocument: Portfolio concentration report

variables.name: Bucket commitments
variables.definition: Commitments already in the bucket.
variables.sourceDocument: Portfolio concentration report

inExcel.note: Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: More headroom is safer. A negative result means the bucket is already over its cap. Caps are in the Model Credit Policy, Concentration, exceptions and approval authority.
commonSlips: Is headroom just cap × base − bucket? No. The new loan also grows the base, so divide by (1 − cap).
Balances or commitments? Commitments.
takeaways: Headroom = (cap × base − bucket) ÷ (1 − cap).
The new loan grows the base too.
Negative headroom means committee for any new loan.

name: Cash-on-cash return
whatItIs: Cash-on-cash return is the owner's yearly cash flow after debt service, as a share of the cash they put in. It answers: what does the borrower earn on their own money? It is the borrower's measure, not a credit test.
analogy: It is the interest your own savings earn after the bank takes its share.

variables.name: Net operating income
variables.definition: Yearly income before debt service.
variables.sourceDocument: T-12 operating statement

variables.name: Annual debt service
variables.definition: Twelve rounded monthly payments.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Cash invested
variables.definition: The owner's cash in the deal; here value less loan.
variables.sourceDocument: Appraisal excerpt (value) and term sheet (loan)

inExcel.note: Keep the ratio unrounded and format the cell as a percentage. Compare it with a limit at full precision. Use ROUND only in a separate display cell.

readTheResult: No policy limit applies. A return below the cap rate signals negative leverage: the loan costs more than the property yields. A thin or negative return can weaken the sponsor's will to support the deal.
commonSlips: Did I take off debt service? Without it you get the cap rate, not the owner's return.
Do I divide by value or price? No. Divide by the cash invested.
takeaways: Cash-on-cash = (income − debt service) ÷ cash invested.
Below the cap rate means negative leverage.
It is a borrower measure; no policy minimum applies.

name: Present and future value
libraryName: Present and future value (time value of money) (SUGGESTED)
whatItIs: Present value is what a stream of future payments is worth today at a given rate. It answers: what is this loan worth now, or what will today's money grow to? It underlies payment, balance and yield formulas.
analogy: It is asking how much you must deposit today to fund a set of future bills.

variables.name: Level payment
variables.definition: The payment at the end of each period.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Lump sum at the end
variables.definition: A balloon or payoff paid with the last payment.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Rate per period
variables.definition: The annual rate ÷ 12 for monthly payments.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Number of periods
variables.definition: How many payments.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: Excel's PV assumes end-of-period payments, as this formula does. Keep the result cell unrounded and format it for display. If you need a rounded figure, put =ROUND(cell,2) in a separate display cell that no other formula uses.

readTheResult: At the note rate, a loan's payments are worth its amount. Discount them at a higher rate and they are worth less. No policy limit applies.
commonSlips: Can I use the annual rate for monthly payments? No. Divide by 12 first.
Payments at the start or end of the month? This formula assumes the end.
Did I leave out the balloon? An interest-only loan's value is mostly its final payoff.
takeaways: Present value = payments × annuity factor + lump sum discounted.
At the note rate, a loan is worth its amount.
Use the rate per period and the right number of periods.

name: Effective annual rate
libraryName: Effective annual rate from a nominal rate (SUGGESTED)
whatItIs: The effective annual rate is what a quoted rate really costs over a year, after day count and compounding. It answers: are two loans with the same quote really the same price?
analogy: It is the price per kilo once you read the small print on pack size.

variables.name: Nominal annual rate
variables.definition: The rate quoted in the note.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Days of accrual a year
variables.definition: 365 (366 in a leap year) for Actual/360; 360 for 30/360.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Payments a year
variables.definition: How often interest is paid or added to principal.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: Format three decimals. Keep the ratio unrounded and format the cell as a percentage. Compare it with a limit at full precision. Use ROUND only in a separate display cell.

readTheResult: A higher effective rate means a dearer loan. Compare loans on it, but never use it in coverage or sizing tests, which use the nominal rate. No policy limit applies.
commonSlips: Can I use it in a coverage test? No. Tests use the nominal rate.
Interest is paid only at maturity. Do I still compound monthly? No. Set payments a year to 1.
takeaways: Effective rate = (1 + rate × days ÷ 360 ÷ m)^m − 1.
Actual/360 billing adds about 1.4% of the rate.
Compare loans on it; test loans on the nominal rate.

name: Remaining balance after k payments
libraryName: Remaining loan balance after k payments (SUGGESTED)
whatItIs: This is the principal still owed after a number of scheduled payments, on a note that accrues on 30/360. It answers: how big is the balloon at maturity? A short term on a long amortization leaves a large one.
analogy: It is how much of the mountain is still above you after a set number of steps.

variables.name: Original loan
variables.definition: The loan at the start.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Monthly rate
variables.definition: The annual rate ÷ 12.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Monthly payment
variables.definition: The scheduled payment, rounded to the cent.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Payments made
variables.definition: Number of payments so far, for example to maturity.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: ROUND in B4 is the payment rule, not display. Keep B6 unrounded; format it for display.

readTheResult: A smaller balloon is safer, because the borrower must refinance or sell to pay it. Size the take-out on it. For notes that accrue on actual days, use the Actual/360 balance instead.
commonSlips: Can I use the unrounded payment? No. The schedule uses the rounded payment, so the balance drifts by cents.
Is the balance the payoff? No. Payoff adds accrued interest and fees.
takeaways: Balance = loan grown at the rate − payments grown at the rate.
Use the payment rounded to the cent.
It suits 30/360 notes; Actual/360 notes need the month-by-month balance.

name: Internal rate of return
whatItIs: The internal rate of return is the one rate that makes a set of cash flows worth zero today. It answers: what yield does the lender really earn, once points and timing count? Points raise it above the note rate.
analogy: It is the steady interest rate a savings account would need to match the deal's cash flows.

variables.name: Cash flow in period t
variables.definition: Money out (negative) or in (positive) for the lender in each period.
variables.sourceDocument: Term sheet and note (amount, points, rate, term)

variables.name: Period
variables.definition: The month the cash flow falls in, from 0.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Periods a year
variables.definition: 12 for monthly flows.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: IRR returns a monthly rate. Format the results to three decimals. Keep the ratio unrounded and format the cell as a percentage. Compare it with a limit at full precision. Use ROUND only in a separate display cell.

readTheResult: A higher yield is better for the lender. Points paid up front raise the yield more on a short loan. It is not a state usury test; counsel decides how a state counts fees.
commonSlips: Is the monthly IRR an annual rate? No. Multiply by 12 for nominal, or compound for effective.
Points came off the loan. Do I count them again as income? No. Count each dollar once.
takeaways: The yield is the rate that makes the cash flows' present value zero.
Points push it above the note rate.
Multiply a monthly yield by 12, or compound it.

name: Remaining balance with Actual/360 interest
whatItIs: This is the balance after a number of payments on a note whose payment is set on 30/360 but whose interest accrues on actual days. It answers: how big is the real balloon on a term loan?
analogy: It is a treadmill set a little faster than you walk: you still move forward, but more slowly.

variables.name: Original loan
variables.definition: The loan at the start.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Annual rate
variables.definition: The yearly rate in the note.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Monthly payment
variables.definition: The payment set on 30/360, rounded to the cent.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Days in month t
variables.definition: Actual days in each accrual month.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

variables.name: Payments made
variables.definition: Payments so far.
variables.sourceDocument: Promissory note and loan agreement excerpt

inExcel.note: ROUND in E8 is the note's rule: each month's interest is rounded to the cent once. It is not display rounding. Keep the balance column unrounded beyond that.

readTheResult: A smaller balloon is safer. Size the refinance on this balloon, not the 30/360 one. The payment and accrual rule is in the Model Credit Policy, Pricing structure.
commonSlips: Can I use the 30/360 balance formula? No. It understates the balloon on an Actual/360 note.
Should the payment change each month? No. The payment stays fixed; only interest changes.
Does the start month matter? Yes. Leap years and month lengths change the result.
takeaways: Each month: interest on actual days, rounded to the cent; balance = balance + interest − payment.
The balloon is larger than on 30/360.
Size the take-out on this balance.
